introduction-hardware-vs-system-time.core: Computers have a battery-backed real-time clock (RTC) that keeps time while powered off, and high-resolution counters (TSC, HPET, ACPI PM timer) used while running. At boot the kernel reads the RTC, then keeps system time by counting ticks from the chosen clocksource. All crystals drift (around tens of ppm, seconds per day), so NTP or PTP continuously disciplines system time and periodically writes it back to the RTC.

first_principles.problem: Two servers' logs differ by 4 seconds, making incident timelines impossible to reconstruct.
truths: The kernel counts from a clocksource.

analogy.title: A wristwatch and a radio time signal
analogy.story: Your watch drifts a little each day; tuning to the radio signal keeps it right.
analogy.breaks: Watches drift slowly; VM clocks can jump after pauses.

code.text:
timedatectl
cat /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource   # tsc
hwclock --show
chronyc tracking | grep -E 'System time|Frequency'

check.q: Why can't a server rely on its hardware clock alone for accurate time?
check.a: Crystal oscillators drift (temperature, manufacturing), accumulating seconds of error over days without external correction.

wall-clock-vs-monotonic-clock.core: CLOCK_REALTIME (wall clock) is calendar time and can jump backward or forward when NTP corrects it, an admin sets it, or leap seconds occur, so it's right for timestamps but wrong for measuring durations. CLOCK_MONOTONIC only moves forward at a steady rate (slewed by NTP but never stepped) from an arbitrary start, which suits timeouts, intervals and latency. CLOCK_BOOTTIME also counts suspend. Using wall clock for durations causes negative latencies and broken timeouts.

first_principles.problem: After an NTP step correction, a service computes a negative request duration and its timeout logic fires immediately.
derivation: Never subtract **wall-clock** times for elapsed time.

analogy.title: A calendar clock vs a stopwatch
analogy.story: The wall clock may be reset for daylight saving; a stopwatch only counts elapsed time.
analogy.breaks: Stopwatches stop when you press stop; MONOTONIC keeps running (but not during suspend).

code.text:
import time
start = time.monotonic()
do_work()
elapsed = time.monotonic() - start          # immune to NTP steps
logged_at = time.time()                      # wall clock for timestamp
# bad: time.time() - start_wall can be negative after a clock step

check.q: Why should timeouts use a monotonic clock?
check.a: Wall-clock time can jump due to NTP or manual changes, making timeouts fire early or never.

ntp-and-clock-discipline.core: NTP clients (chrony, ntpd, systemd-timesyncd) query multiple time servers, estimate offset and network delay, filter outliers, and discipline the clock. They slew (gradually adjust frequency) for small offsets, and step only at startup or for large errors, avoiding jumps. chrony handles intermittent networks and VMs well and is the modern default. For microsecond accuracy, PTP with hardware timestamping is used; cloud providers offer local time services (169.254.169.123 on AWS).

first_principles.problem: Database replicas reject writes due to clock skew because NTP was misconfigured on half the nodes.

analogy.title: Asking several people the time and averaging
analogy.story: You discount the one who's clearly wrong, then nudge your watch gradually instead of jumping it.
analogy.breaks: People answer instantly; NTP must account for network delay.

code.text:
# /etc/chrony/chrony.conf
server 169.254.169.123 prefer iburst minpoll 4 maxpoll 4
pool 2.pool.ntp.org iburst
makestep 1.0 3
rtcsync
# chronyc tracking → System time: 0.000012 seconds fast of NTP time

check.q: What's the difference between slewing and stepping the clock?
check.a: Slewing gradually adjusts clock speed to correct small offsets without jumps; stepping sets the time instantly, causing jumps.

leap-seconds-and-leap-smearing.core: Leap seconds keep UTC aligned with Earth's rotation by occasionally inserting a 61st second (23:59:60). Software often assumes 60-second minutes, and kernels historically stepped or repeated a second, causing livelocks and crashes (the 2012 incidents). Leap smearing (Google, AWS, Meta) spreads the extra second over hours by slightly slowing clocks, so there's no discontinuity. Don't mix smeared and non-smeared time sources, and note that leap seconds are planned to be abolished by 2035.

first_principles.problem: On a leap second night, Java and MySQL processes spin at 100% CPU on many servers.
truths: UTC occasionally needs an extra second.

analogy.title: Adding an extra minute to a race by slowing everyone a little all day
analogy.story: Instead of a sudden pause, every lap is slightly longer, and nobody notices.
analogy.breaks: Races have one clock; mixed time sources disagree during a smear.

code.text:
# all nodes use the same smeared source (AWS Time Sync Service smears leap seconds)
server 169.254.169.123 prefer iburst
# do NOT also list pool.ntp.org (non-smeared) on the same hosts
# chronyc sources → single consistent source

check.q: Why is mixing smeared and non-smeared NTP sources dangerous?
check.a: During a leap smear they disagree by up to a second, confusing clients and causing clock jumps or inconsistent time across hosts.

time-namespaces.core: Time namespaces (Linux 5.6+) let processes see offsets for CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME, so a container's uptime and monotonic clock can start near zero or be shifted. That's mainly used for container checkpoint and restore and migration (CRIU), where restored processes must see continuous monotonic time on a new host. Wall-clock (REALTIME) can't be namespaced, so system time stays global and changing it needs CAP_SYS_TIME on the host.

first_principles.problem: After live-migrating a checkpointed container, its monotonic timers jump because the new host's uptime differs.

analogy.title: Resetting a stopwatch display for a relocated runner
analogy.story: The runner keeps their own elapsed time even though the new stadium's clock shows something else.
analogy.breaks: Stopwatches are personal; wall-clock time stays shared.

code.text:
unshare --time --fork --boottime 86400 --monotonic 86400 cat /proc/uptime
# shows uptime ~1 day larger than host
cat /proc/self/timens_offsets

check.q: Which clocks can be offset in a Linux time namespace?
check.a: CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME; CLOCK_REALTIME remains global.
